items.name: Ruth Ellington
items.summary: Weston said Duke Ellington's sister Ruth Ellington only wanted to hear him play solo piano and would not hear him any other way.
items.one_liner: duke's sister, who only wanted his solo piano
items.his_quote: Duke Ellington’s sister, Ruth Ellington; she didn’t want to hear me any other way.

more_his_quotes.quote: Duke’s sister, she only wanted to hear me play solo piano.

items.notes: Named once (309882) and referred to unnamed as "Duke's sister" in 309856. She evidently heard him play and stated a preference, so some acquaintance is implied, but the nature of their contact is not described.

items.name: Maurice Cullaz
items.identity_note: Upstream Q1293705 (French jazz journalist, 1912–2000) fits the Paris context.
items.summary: Weston mentioned Maurice Cullaz only to identify his wife in Paris, who he said only wanted to hear him play solo piano.
items.one_liner: his wife in paris loved weston's solo piano
items.his_quote: Maurice Cullaz’s wife in Paris, she only wanted to hear me solo piano.
items.notes: The sentence is about Cullaz's (unnamed) wife, not Cullaz himself; naming her by her husband implies Weston knew the couple, but no contact with Maurice is stated. A human may prefer 'acquaintance of'.

items.name: Cole Porter
items.summary: Weston said his first recording, for Riverside, was of Cole Porter's music, done as piano and bass with Sam Gill after he argued against a solo album.
items.one_liner: his music was weston's first riverside record
items.his_quote: So, my first recording of Cole Porter was piano and bass, but they wanted me to do solo piano.
items.notes: Upstream evidence quoted the wrong sentence (the royalty-of-piano list, which does not name Porter); the relation 'knows of' is still right. 'composer' role is implied by 'recording of Cole Porter'.

items.name: Billy Harper
items.identity_note: Transcript has "Billy Hopper" (309885) in the sextet he took to Morocco; two blocks later (309887) the same trip names "Billy Harper", the tenor saxophonist named throughout the interview. Mishearing of Harper.
items.summary: Weston named Billy Harper in the sextet he brought to Morocco for the film "Randy in Tangiers" and said he was the only one who was cool riding donkeys up to Jajouka, being from Texas.
items.one_liner: the only one cool riding donkeys to jajouka
items.his_quote: Billy Harper was the only one that was cool, because Billy, being from Texas, he knew how to ride horses and donkeys.

more_his_quotes.quote: Eric Asante, African percussion from Ghana I had Benny Powell, and I had Billy Hopper.

items.notes: Fold into the Billy Harper entry. The his_quote is spelled 'Harper' in the transcript (309887), same trip.

items.name: Eric Asante
items.summary: Weston named Eric Asante, from Ghana, as the African percussionist in the sextet he brought to Morocco for the film "Randy in Tangiers".
items.one_liner: ghanaian percussionist in his sextet in morocco
items.his_quote: Eric Asante, African percussion from Ghana I had Benny Powell, and I had Billy Hopper.
items.notes: Roll-call only; the punctuation run-on ('from Ghana I had Benny Powell') is the transcriber's.

items.name: Alan Hayward
items.summary: Weston named Alan Hayward as the drummer in the sextet he brought to Morocco for the film "Randy in Tangiers".
items.one_liner: drummer in his sextet in morocco
items.his_quote: I brought the sextet over Alan Hayward on drums

more_his_quotes.quote: So when we got to the staging place where you start to go up the mountain, here you got Al Hayward, you got all the guys, you know?

items.notes: Same person as 'Al Hayward' in 309887 (same trip, same band). Spelling of surname not verifiable from the transcript.

items.name: Tom McKenzie
items.summary: Weston, having forgotten the bass player of the sextet he took to Morocco, later remembered him as Tom McKenzie while describing the band riding donkeys up the mountain to Jajouka.
items.one_liner: bassist who rode a donkey up to jajouka
items.his_quote: Tom McKenzie was the bass player. Seeing these guys going up the mountains on these donkeys, with their instruments, that was incredible.

more_his_quotes.quote: on bass was…how did I forget the bass player? It’ll come back to me.

items.notes: Upstream placed him in the 1972 Tangiers festival band; wrong — he is the bassist of the later sextet trip for the 'Randy in Tangiers' film (309885/309887), whose name Weston had forgotten a block earlier. No date for that trip is given.

items.name: Azzedine Weston
items.identity_note: No QID; Weston names him as 'my son Azzedine'.
items.summary: Weston said his son Azzedine played percussion at the 1972 festival he organised at a bullring in Tangiers.
items.one_liner: his son; percussion at the 1972 tangiers festival
items.his_quote: We organized this festival and I brought over Odetta, Max Roach’s without Max: Cecil Bridgewater, Billy Harper, Junior Booth, my son Azzedine played percussion.
items.notes: Family member, so relation 'none' per spec although he played in the festival. 309856 ('Steve Berrios on percussion cause my son couldn’t make it', 1974) almost certainly refers to the same son but does not name him.

items.name: Al Hayward
items.summary: Weston named Al Hayward among the band members who had to ride donkeys up the mountain to Jajouka during the "Randy in Tangiers" trip.
items.one_liner: drummer on the donkey ride to jajouka
items.his_quote: So when we got to the staging place where you start to go up the mountain, here you got Al Hayward, you got all the guys, you know?

more_his_quotes.quote: I brought the sextet over Alan Hayward on drums

items.notes: Same person as 'Alan Hayward' (drums) in 309885. Upstream dated this to 1972; wrong — this is the later film trip, not the 1972 festival.

items.name: Junior Booth
items.summary: Weston named Junior Booth among the members of Max Roach's band, without Max, whom he brought to his 1972 festival in Tangiers.
items.one_liner: max roach's band at his 1972 tangiers festival
items.his_quote: We organized this festival and I brought over Odetta, Max Roach’s without Max: Cecil Bridgewater, Billy Harper, Junior Booth, my son Azzedine played percussion.
items.notes: Upstream called him a percussionist; the transcript gives no instrument (the percussion clause belongs to Azzedine). Probably the bassist Junie Booth, who worked with Max Roach — check. The transcript does not say Weston played with this band, only that he brought it over, so 'acquaintance of' rather than a music relation.

items.name: Cecil Bridgewater
items.identity_note: Q1052278 (American jazz trumpeter, b. 1942) fits: he played with Max Roach's band.
items.summary: Weston named Cecil Bridgewater first among the members of Max Roach's band, without Max, whom he brought to his 1972 festival in Tangiers.
items.one_liner: max roach's band at his 1972 tangiers festival
items.his_quote: We organized this festival and I brought over Odetta, Max Roach’s without Max: Cecil Bridgewater, Billy Harper, Junior Booth, my son Azzedine played percussion.
items.notes: Weston brought the band over as festival organiser; the transcript does not say he performed with them, so 'acquaintance of' rather than 'collaborated with'. No instrument given in the transcript.

items.name: Max Roach
items.summary: Weston said he brought Max Roach's band, without Max himself, to his 1972 festival in Tangiers.
items.one_liner: his band came to tangiers without him
items.his_quote: We organized this festival and I brought over Odetta, Max Roach’s without Max: Cecil Bridgewater, Billy Harper, Junior Booth, my son Azzedine played percussion.
items.notes: 'Max Roach’s without Max' — a word (band/group) seems dropped by speaker or transcriber. Booking his band implies dealings with Roach, but no contact with him is stated.

items.name: Pucho (Henry "Pucho" Brown)
items.identity_note: No QID. 'Pucho' is the leader of Pucho and His Latin Soul Brothers (Henry 'Pucho' Brown, timbalero); the transcript names only the band.
items.summary: Weston listed Pucho and His Latin Soul Brothers among the acts at the three-day festival he organised in Tangiers in 1972.
items.one_liner: his band played weston's 1972 tangiers festival
items.his_quote: Mandrill, and Pucho and His Latin Soul Brothers, and we had 40 African musicians.

more_his_quotes.quote: We had this three-day festival at a bullring in Tangiers.

items.notes: Only the band name occurs; 'Pucho' as an individual is the bandleader. Could reasonably be typed is_person false (group). The relation rests on Weston being the festival organiser; no personal contact is described.

items.name: Mandrill
items.notes: Mandrill is a band (Brooklyn funk/Latin-soul group), listed among the acts at Weston's 1972 Tangiers festival (309887–309888).

items.name: Archbishop of Canterbury
items.notes: A title, not a named individual. Jenkins raised 'your experience with the Arch Bishop of Canterbury'; Weston described playing at Canterbury with three Gnawa for a meeting of spiritual leaders arranged by Zeba Rachman (309889–309892), but never says he met the Archbishop personally. No date given, so the office-holder cannot be identified from the transcript.

items.name: Zeyba Rahman
items.identity_note: Transcript has 'Zeba' (Weston, 309890), 'Rahman?' (Jenkins, 309891) and 'Rachman' (Weston, 309892). Read as Zeyba Rahman, the India-born curator of sacred and Sufi music programmes; spelling of both names is by ear. Not certain — check.
items.summary: Weston said a woman from India, Zeba Rachman, arranged for him and three Gnawa from Tangiers to play for a meeting of spiritual leaders at Canterbury.
items.one_liner: arranged his canterbury performance with three gnawa
items.his_quote: Well, that was organized by a woman from India, Zeba…

more_his_quotes.quote: Rachman, and she arranged for us… they were having a meeting of spiritual leaders from all over the world and the Arch Bishop of Canterbury in England. So she arranged for myself, and three Gnawa from Tangiers and leaders from everywhere.

items.notes: Same person as 'Rahman' (Jenkins's prompt) and 'Rachman' (Weston's reply). Jenkins supplied the surname; Weston repeated it with a slightly different spelling.

items.name: Zeyba Rahman
items.identity_note: Jenkins's 'Rahman' is the surname of the woman Weston called 'Zeba' (309890) and then 'Rachman' (309892); read as Zeyba Rahman — check.
items.summary: Jenkins supplied the surname Rahman for the woman from India whom Weston said arranged his Canterbury performance with three Gnawa; Weston accepted it as 'Rachman'.
items.one_liner: arranged his canterbury performance with three gnawa
items.his_quote: Rachman, and she arranged for us…
items.notes: Duplicate of 'Zeba'/'Rachman'. Basis is his_statement because the relationship (she arranged the event) is Weston's own words; only the surname came from Jenkins.

items.name: Zeyba Rahman
items.identity_note: Transcript 'Rachman' (Weston) answers Jenkins's 'Rahman?'; read as Zeyba Rahman, the India-born sacred-music curator — check.
items.summary: Weston said Rachman, a woman from India, arranged for him and three Gnawa from Tangiers to play for a meeting of spiritual leaders at Canterbury.
items.one_liner: arranged his canterbury performance with three gnawa
items.his_quote: Rachman, and she arranged for us… they were having a meeting of spiritual leaders from all over the world and the Arch Bishop of Canterbury in England. So she arranged for myself, and three Gnawa from Tangiers and leaders from everywhere.

more_his_quotes.quote: Well, that was organized by a woman from India, Zeba…

items.notes: Same person as 'Zeba' (309890) and Jenkins's 'Rahman' (309891). She organised the event; she is not a musician, so 'collaborated with' (upstream) overstates it.

items.name: Salah Ragab
items.identity_note: Q2213803 (Egyptian drummer, 1935–2008) fits: Weston says in 2009 that he 'died last year' and led a big band in Cairo.
items.summary: Weston called Salah Ragab, a Cairo big-band leader who played Duke and Basie, a dear friend whose death he learned of only months later, and said Ragab got him invited to play the opening of the new library in Alexandria.
items.one_liner: dear friend; got him the alexandria library opening
items.his_quote: Yeah, a dear friend of mine, in fact he died last year and I didn’t find out until two months ago, his name is Salah Ragab.

more_his_quotes.quote: has a big band. He plays Duke, Basie, everything. He was a good friend of mine. We were in Egypt and we spent time with him, my wife and I.
He thought I should be there so what he did was he contacted the director of music in Egypt and the director of the library in Alexandria.

items.name: Stafford James
items.identity_note: Q2328781 (American bassist, b. 1946) is the person Jenkins meant; Weston rejected him as the bassist in question.
items.summary: Jenkins suggested Stafford James as the Paris-based bassist who played with Weston at the Alexandria library opening, and Weston said it was not him.
items.his_quote: No, not Stafford. It’ll come to me.
items.notes: Rejected guess. Nothing in the transcript establishes any relation; upstream 'knows of' is not supported. The bassist at Alexandria is never named.

items.name: the Queen
items.notes: A title for an unnamed head of state at the opening of the library in Alexandria (309901). The transcript does not say which queen; Weston only lists her among the heads of state who attended.

items.name: Arab singers
items.notes: A generic group: most of the other performers at the Alexandria library opening (309901).

items.name: President of Greece
items.notes: A title for the unnamed Greek head of state at the opening of the library in Alexandria (309901). If that is the 2002 Bibliotheca Alexandrina opening it would be Konstantinos Stephanopoulos, but the transcript gives no date — outside inference only.

items.name: President of Egypt
items.notes: A title for the unnamed Egyptian head of state at the opening of the library in Alexandria (309901) — presumably Hosni Mubarak, but the transcript does not name him.

items.name: Fatoumata Mbengue
items.identity_note: No QID. Surface forms 'Fatu' (Jenkins, 309902), 'Fatou' (309909–309911) and 'Fatoumata Mbengue' (309907) are the same woman, his wife.
items.era: married after his NEA Jazz Masters award
items.summary: Weston said he met his wife Fatoumata Mbengue, a Lebou/Wolof woman from Senegal with an African shop in Paris, through Gnawa who invited her to his Paris concert, and that he suddenly declared he wanted to marry her in Egypt, where they wed in a Nubian ceremony.
items.one_liner: his wife; married in a nubian village ceremony
items.his_quote: Well, what happened was, I met my wife, Fatoumata Mbengue. She’s a Lebo woman, Wulluf, from Senegal. She has a beautiful African shop in Paris.

more_his_quotes.quote: I passed her shop many times and never went in for some reason, but I realized when I went in that that was it; I’d never come out again.
I told this guy, “I want to marry this woman.” I don’t know where it came from.
We did a Nubian ceremony, a Nubian marriage. It was something, some kind of adventure.
At the time “Saga” came, actually, from the name of an African shop that my wife, who I married afterwards, her shop was called “Saga”.

items.notes: Upstream's 'in music group with … musical collaborator (Gnawa)' is wrong: she is his wife, introduced via Gnawa musicians. Also referred to as 'my wife' in 309813 (her shop 'Saga' gave the 1995 album its title), 309897, 309915. The second Egypt trip was 'right after I got my Jazz Masters grant'.

items.name: Wolof
items.notes: 'Wulluf' is the Wolof people of Senegal, describing Fatoumata Mbengue's ethnicity ('She’s a Lebo woman, Wulluf, from Senegal', 309907). 'Lebo' = Lebou.

items.name: Ariane Smolderen
items.summary: Weston said the Belgian photographer Ariane Smolderen travelled Morocco with him photographing a history of Gnawa families, and that through her he was invited to a conference on Sufi music in Egypt.
items.one_liner: photographed gnawa families with him across morocco
items.his_quote: What happened was, because I was invited because a photographer named Ariane Smolderen, she’s from Belgium; we made trips to Morocco to photograph a history of the Gnawa people.

more_his_quotes.quote: We traveled Fez, to Marrakech, to Telouet, to Agadir, we went down the Sahara just photographing Gnawa families, because there are different parts of Morocco.

items.notes: 'Collaborated with' here is a photographic project, not music. The sentences after are ambiguous about who 'knew my interests in Sufism' — Smolderen or her friend, a Belgian gallery owner in Paris.

items.name: Ramsey
items.summary: Weston said the Egyptian taxi driver Ramsey, whom he would never forget, threw out the taxi's seat to give him legroom and broke away from the tourist convoy to drive him and Fatou to Aswan.
items.one_liner: taxi driver who threw out the seat
items.his_quote: We talked to the taxi cab driver to take us, Ramsey, I’ll never forget him. He took the seat out of the taxi and made sure I had a lot of legroom, he threw the whole seat out!

more_his_quotes.quote: So finally Ramsey says, “Look, let’s get away from this convoy.” So we left the convoy and we drove to Azwan.

items.notes: Probably the Egyptian name Ramzi; left as transcribed. Upstream 'acquaintance of' overstates a single journey.

items.name: Shadley
items.summary: Weston said Shadley, an inspector of antiquities who approached him and Fatou at the temple of Isis in Aswan, showed them round and introduced them to the head of the Nubian museum, and on a later trip arranged their Nubian wedding when Weston suddenly told him he wanted to marry her.
items.one_liner: guided him at isis temple; arranged his wedding
items.his_quote: he says, “My name is Shadley, I’m with the inspectors of antiquity of Egyptian art.” He said, “I’d like to take you around.”

more_his_quotes.quote: So he took us and we went to the Nubian museum. He introduced us to the head of the Nubian museum in Aswan.
So, with that wonderful tribute they gave me we went back to Egypt and we saw this guy again.
This guy said, “Okay.” He took us to this Nubian village and took us to get jewelry, took us to get photographs and dress us in Nubian clothes.

items.notes: He is named only once; 'this guy' who arranged the wedding (309910–309911) is read as the same man from 'we saw this guy again' — check. Upstream 'has met' understates two trips and the wedding.

items.name: Imam
items.notes: A religious title, not a name: 'Her grandfather was an Imam' (309911) — Fatoumata Mbengue's unnamed grandfather.

items.name: John Lewis
items.identity_note: Q353943 (pianist, MJQ, 1920–2001) is right: he was a 2001 NEA Jazz Master alongside Weston and Jackie McLean.
items.summary: Jenkins noted that John Lewis was named an NEA Jazz Master in the same year as Weston; Weston did not mention him.
items.interviewer_quote: You were selected along with Jackie McLean and John Lewis.
items.notes: Jenkins dates the award to 2003; the archive header (309808) says 2001 — Jenkins's date looks wrong. Weston answers only about what the award meant to him.

items.name: Jackie McLean
items.identity_note: Q920490 (alto saxophonist, 1931–2006) is right: a 2001 NEA Jazz Master with Weston.
items.summary: Jenkins noted that Jackie McLean was named an NEA Jazz Master in the same year as Weston; Weston did not mention him.
items.interviewer_quote: You were selected along with Jackie McLean and John Lewis.
items.notes: Jenkins says 2003; the header (309808) says 2001.

items.name: Billie Holiday
items.summary: Weston counted Billie Holiday among the ancestors who made the music under segregation, said he sat opposite her to shake her hand, and named "Portrait of Billie Holliday" among the three compositions of his "Three African Queens" (1991).
items.one_liner: sat opposite her to shake her hand
items.his_quote: I sat opposite of Billie Holiday to shake her hand.

more_his_quotes.quote: But those people! God bless them, and I’ve met most of them, you know?
Okay, what happened was in 1991 I was very fortunate to write three compositions: “Portrait of Billie Holliday”, “Blues for Elma Lewis”, and a royal lady. And it was entitled “Three African Queens”

items.notes: Also appears as the tune title 'Portrait of Billie Holliday' (309822, spelled with two l's) — same person; not in the input as a separate entry. Era field: the handshake is undated.

items.name: Paul Robeson
items.identity_note: Transcript has 'Paul Robinson' (309915): a man whose hand Weston shook at a New York ballroom, listed among the African American heroes of his youth — read as Paul Robeson, a known mishearing in this transcript (spec). No upstream QID.
items.summary: Weston said he shook Paul Robeson's hand at a ballroom in New York City, repeating it among the heroes whose struggle produced the music.
items.one_liner: shook his hand at a new york ballroom
items.his_quote: I shook Paul Robinson’s hand at a ballroom in New York City. I shook Paul’s hand.

more_his_quotes.quote: But those people! God bless them, and I’ve met most of them, you know?

items.notes: Mentioned once; the repetition 'I shook Paul’s hand' is his emphasis.

items.name: Dinah Washington
items.identity_note: Transcript has 'Diana Washington' (309915), named with Louis Jordan and Nat King Cole as Black stars who made it through segregation — read as the singer Dinah Washington.
items.summary: Weston named Dinah Washington, with Louis Jordan and Nat King Cole, among the Black artists whose achievement under segregation amazed him: "How did Diana Washington do it?"
items.one_liner: one of the elders whose achievement amazes him
items.his_quote: Everyday that I’m home I look at my mother and father and I say, “How did y’all do it? How did Louie Jordan do it? How did Nat King Cole do it? How did Diana Washington do it?”
items.notes: Later in the block he says of 'those people' that 'I’ve met most of them', which could include her, but no meeting with her specifically is stated.

items.name: Louis Jordan
items.identity_note: Transcript has 'Louie Jordan' (309915), the same by-ear spelling as 'Louie Armstrong'; read as the bandleader Louis Jordan.
items.summary: Weston named Louis Jordan, with Nat King Cole and Dinah Washington, among the Black artists whose achievement under segregation amazed him: "How did Louie Jordan do it?"
items.one_liner: one of the elders whose achievement amazes him
items.his_quote: Everyday that I’m home I look at my mother and father and I say, “How did y’all do it? How did Louie Jordan do it? How did Nat King Cole do it? How did Diana Washington do it?”
items.notes: Upstream evidence spliced in Louis Armstrong's handshake, which is a different person. 'I’ve met most of them' later in the block is not specific to Jordan.

items.summary: Kyle Kelly-Yahner transcribed the interview and is never mentioned by Weston.
